plot_extraction.response_text:
Two broke bushmen, Dave Regan and Jim Bently, encounter drovers waiting near Mulgatown to be paid. Knowing that a shrewd publican called Poisonous Jimmy hopes to lure the drovers into spending their cheques, Dave and Jim hide their swags and pose as members of the party. Jimmy gives them free drinks, lends them a sovereign, and sends them away with a can of beer for their supposed mates.

After giving the beer to the real drovers, Dave and Jim secretly bypass the shanty and escape through Mulgatown. When the drovers later pass Jimmy’s place without stopping, he realizes he has been tricked. He pursues them, angrily demands repayment, and starts a fight before learning that the two swindlers never belonged to their group. Enraged, Jimmy gets drunk and sets out after the pair with a tomahawk, but mounted police arrest him, and he is fined.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story adopts the form of an Australian bush yarn: an anecdotal, orally inflected tale built around deception, drink, rough fellowship and an ironic reversal. Its two-part structure retells the same incident from different viewpoints. Dave Regan’s first-person account explains how he and Jim trick the publican, while the second drover’s account reveals the delayed consequences. This overlapping narration creates dramatic irony, broadens the joke and gives the episode the feel of a story passed from speaker to speaker around a campfire.

The narrative voice is informal, companionable and digressive. Both narrators speak as working bushmen addressing an implied audience, frequently using formulas such as “I can tell you a yarn” and pausing to supply local history, gossip or practical explanation. Their voices are observant but understated: dubious conduct is related with little moral anxiety, as though cunning, drinking and minor swindling are ordinary parts of life on the track. The narration generally proceeds chronologically, but compact descriptive asides—especially the explanation of Poisonous Jimmy’s nickname and habits—interrupt the action in the manner of spontaneous oral storytelling.

The diction is strongly vernacular and regionally marked. Australian terms such as “swags,” “mulga,” “mob,” “tucker,” “shanty,” “shout,” “chequeman,” “cut-out” and “on the boose” establish the social and geographical world without formal exposition. Nonstandard grammar and phonetic contractions—“me and my mate,” “ain’t,” “sez,” “knowed,” “borrered,” “comin’,” “waitin’”—differentiate spoken language from the somewhat more standard narrative prose, although even the narration retains colloquial rhythms. Euphemistic printed oaths such as “blanky,” “flamin’,” “crimson” and interrupted dashes evoke vigorous profanity while turning it into part of the comedy.

Syntax is predominantly direct and additive, with clauses linked by “and,” “but,” “so” and “then.” This produces a steady, conversational momentum and mimics speech rather than polished literary narration. Longer sentences often accumulate actions or descriptive details in loose sequence, while dialogue is delivered in short exchanges and repeated formulas: “‘It’s hot.’ ‘It’s hot.’” Such repetition heightens deadpan humour and later becomes comic when the same social ritual is replayed by the drovers. The prose balances brisk scene-setting with extended comic portraiture, especially in the description of Jimmy’s mismatched eyes, broken nose and beard “like a bush fence round a stubble-field.”

Dialogue carries much of the characterization and action. Dave and Jim’s fraud emerges through insinuation, winks and strategically vague answers rather than explicit planning. Poisonous Jimmy’s calculated hospitality is exposed through his offhand questions, free drinks and conspicuous attempts to appear innocent. In the second half, his mounting fury is conveyed through fractured speech, extravagant abuse and repeated demands for his money. Individual voices are socially specific, but the dialogue also works theatrically, with compact cues, reversals and recurring phrases that resemble the beats of a comic performance.

Characterization relies on caricature, physical detail and behaviour rather than psychological analysis. Dave and Jim are opportunistic, quick-witted and laconic. The drovers are rough but fair-minded, willing both to drink Jimmy’s beer and to pay for it when challenged. Jimmy is the central comic figure: predatory, suspicious and physically formidable, yet defeated by his own greed. His “sharp cunning little eye” and misleading “cold stony eye” become a running motif, first suggesting menace and later complicating the fight. Minor figures—the flirtatious barmaid, the quiet boss and the mounted police—are sketched economically through a gesture, manner or role.

The humour is dry, cumulative and ironic. Much of it comes from incongruous similes, restrained commentary and the gap between what Jimmy thinks is happening and what the reader knows. His smile is so false it would make “anybody home-sick”; his beard resembles a rough fence; his grin is “like a parson with a broken nose.” The deception succeeds because Jimmy believes he is manipulating the supposed drovers, only to discover that his own bait—free beer and credit—has been used against him. The anticlimactic final sentence, “They fined him ten bob,” compresses Jimmy’s rage, pursuit and claims of justice into a flat bureaucratic punchline.

The setting is rendered through practical details of distance, heat, dust, money, horses, cattle and roadside drinking places. The landscape is not treated lyrically; it is a working environment that determines thirst, travel, employment and vulnerability. Social life revolves around droving camps, stores, shanties and towns, while money arrives irregularly in cheques and is quickly threatened by alcohol. The story’s world is masculine, itinerant and governed less by formal institutions than by reputation, physical competence and bush codes of reciprocity.

Tonally, the piece is affectionate, sardonic and unsentimental. It does not condemn the swindle directly, but frames it as a contest between habitual tricksters in which the sharper men win. Violence remains comic rather than tragic, and even Jimmy’s threats are absorbed into the exuberance of the yarn. Overall, the style combines oral realism, regional idiom, economical plotting, grotesque comic description and a circular structure in which repeated details acquire fresh meaning from a second teller’s perspective.

### POISONOUS JIMMY’S SHOUT

I can tell you a yarn about me and Jim Bently and a publican they called Poisonous Jimmy, though his proper name was James Phelan, and he kept a shanty five miles the other side of Mulgatown, on the Old Stock Route.

It was a slab place with a bark roof and a verandah that leaned forward as if it was tired of standing, and there was nothing within twenty miles except mulga, dust, and Jimmy’s whisky. The whisky was the worst of the lot.

They called him Poisonous partly on account of the whisky and partly on account of his temper. He had one sharp little eye that looked into you and counted your money, and another pale, stony eye that seemed to be watching somebody behind you. He’d got that eye through being struck with a bottle in Bourke, or kicked by a horse at Cobar, according to whether he was talking to a magistrate or a horseman. His nose had been broken in two places and had set out to the west; and his beard went round his face like a bush fence round a stubble-field. When he smiled—which was mostly when a chequeman came along—the smile would have made anybody home-sick.

Me and Jim was hard up at the time. We’d been sinking tanks for a contractor who went insolvent the day before pay-day, and we had our swags, a plug of tobacco between us, and threepence. The threepence belonged to Jim, but I was helping him look after it.

We was tramping towards Mulgatown in the heat when we came on a mob of travelling cattle camped by a dry creek. There was six drovers and a cook, and they were waiting for the boss to ride in from town with their cheques. They’d been paid off from a Queensland trip and were going south after the cut-out.

One of them knew Jim.

“Any tucker?” sez Jim.

“A bit,” sez he. “Sit down.”

They gave us beef and johnny-cake and tea, and we heard all about the cheques. The boss had promised to be back by sundown. The men meant to pass Poisonous Jimmy’s next morning and go straight through Mulgatown, because they knowed Jimmy’s ways.

“He’ll be waitin’ for us,” said the cook.

“He generally is,” I said.

“He was outside sweeping the road when we come up,” said another chap. “Said he was cleanin’ the place.”

“That road ain’t been swept since the blacks had it,” said Jim.

After dinner we shouldered our swags and started on. We hadn’t gone half a mile when Jim stopped.

“It’s hot,” he said.

“It’s hot,” I said.

“There’ll be beer at Jimmy’s.”

“There generally is—if you’ve got money.”

Jim looked back at the drovers’ camp, and then at me.

“They’re waitin’ for their cheques,” he said.

“They are.”

“And Jimmy’s waitin’ for them.”

“He is.”

Jim shifted his swag to the other shoulder.

“We might as well tell him they’re comin’.”

“We’d be doin’ him a kindness,” I said.

So we went into the mulga and planted our swags under a fallen tree. You can generally tell a sundowner by his swag, and we didn’t want to be taken for anything poorer than drovers. Then we brushed the dust off each other, tightened our belts, and walked on with our hands loose and easy, like men with wages behind them.

Poisonous Jimmy was standing in the road when we came in sight. He was shading his good eye with one hand and pretending not to be looking past us. There was a new blackboard outside the shanty, and on it was written:

**GOOD STABLING. BEST BRANDS. CIVILITY.**

There wasn’t a stable, the brands was Jimmy’s, and civility depended on the amount of your cheque.

“Afternoon,” he said careless-like.

“Afternoon,” I said.

“Hot.”

“It’s hot.”

“Come far?”

“A bit.”

“Cattle travelling slow?”

“Pretty slow,” I said.

He glanced along the road behind us, but the dust hid the camp.

“Better have a drink,” he said. “It’s a dry stretch.”

“We ain’t got time,” said Jim.

That settled it. If we’d said we wanted one, he’d have charged double; but a man in a hurry is nearly always expected to have money.

“Oh, come in,” said Jimmy. “One won’t hurt you.”

We went in.

There was a barmaid called Rosie, a red-haired girl who had been in Mulgatown long enough to know what questions not to ask. She looked at our trousers and boots, then at Jimmy, and began polishing a glass that wasn’t worth it.

“What’ll it be?” said Jimmy.

“Anything,” I said, in the tone of a man who had drunk everything.

He drew three beers and put his own down without paying for it.

“Here’s luck,” he said.

“Here’s luck,” we said.

He drank and watched us over the top of the glass with his sharp eye. The cold eye appeared to be watching the door.

“Boss behind?” he asked after a while.

“He was behind when we left him,” said Jim.

“How many in the party?”

“Oh, the usual mob.”

“Good trip?”

“Fair.”

“Paid off?”

“He went in about the cheques,” I said.

Jimmy’s beard shifted with his smile.

“Have another.”

“We don’t mind.”

We had another, and Jimmy talked about rain, cattle prices, the Government, and the crookedness of publicans in general. He said a man on the road ought to be treated like a Christian. Then he took us through to the dining-room and made Rosie put cold mutton and bread on the table.

“Have a feed,” he said. “No charge.”

“That’s very kind,” said Jim, as if kindness worried him.

“Oh, we always look after the boys here,” said Jimmy.

Rosie turned her back and coughed.

After the feed we went to the bar again. Jimmy was becoming anxious because the drovers hadn’t come in sight, but he didn’t like to show it.

“They’ll be here before dark, I suppose?”

“Likely,” I said.

“Might camp this side?”

“They might.”

“Boss carrying the cheques?”

“I never looked in his pockets.”

Jimmy’s good eye narrowed. Then he smiled again, and it was like a parson smiling through a broken nose.

“Have another drink.”

We had it.

Presently I put my hand into my pocket and looked annoyed.

“What’s up?” said Jim.

“I left me purse in me swag.”

“You always do,” said Jim.

Jimmy heard him.

“Short of a few bob?” he asked.

“Only till the boss comes up,” I said. “I wanted to get some tobacco in Mulgatown.”

“How much?”

“Oh, it don’t matter.”

Jimmy took a sovereign from behind the bar and pushed it towards me. He did it slow, as if his fingers was attached to it by elastic.

“Take that,” he said. “You can square up when the others arrive.”

“I don’t like borrering,” I said.

“You’re all one party, ain’t you?”

Jim looked at me, and I looked at him.

“We’ve been together long enough,” I said.

That answer satisfied Jimmy, because it was true in more ways than he knew. I took the sovereign, and Jimmy wrote something in a book. I reckon he charged interest while he was writing.

“We’d better get back,” said Jim.

“Back?” Jimmy said quickly.

“To see where they’ve got to.”

Jimmy thought a moment, then drew a gallon can of beer and put the lid on it.

“Take this along to the boys,” he said. “Compliments of the house. Tell ’em there’s a good paddock and plenty of water here.”

The paddock was mostly stones and the water had drowned two goats, but we thanked him.

“And tell the boss,” Jimmy added, casual as a snake beside a rabbit-hole, “that I can cash the cheques.”

“We’ll mention it.”

We took the can and walked back along the road. Jimmy stood outside watching us until the bend hid us. Then we cut through the scrub, recovered our swags, and went to the drovers’ camp from the creek side.

“We brought you a present,” said Jim.

The cook opened the can.

“Beer!” he said. “Where’d you get it?”

“Poisonous Jimmy sent it,” I said.

The drovers looked suspicious.

“What for?”

“He’s taken a fancy to you.”

“He ain’t seen us.”

“That’s the beautiful part of it,” said Jim.

We told them enough to make them laugh, but not too much, because a joke can be spoilt by explaining the business side. We drank one pannikin each and left them the rest. Then, while Jimmy was watching the stock-route, me and Jim went across country, skirted the back of his selection, and reached Mulgatown by an old timber track.

We spent sixpence on tobacco, ninepence on tea and meat, and slept beyond the railway dam. Jim said we ought to put the balance aside against Jimmy’s sovereign.

So we put it aside in the Mulgatown Hotel.

That is my part of the yarn.

But I met one of those drovers years afterwards at a shed on the Bogan, and he told me what happened after we left. I’ll give it as near as I remember, because a yarn like this belongs to all hands once it gets started.

* * *

We got our cheques that evening, and the boss had heard things in Mulgatown that made him particular about Poisonous Jimmy. So he sez:

“We’ll start early and go straight through.”

No one objected. We’d drunk Jimmy’s beer and felt friendly towards him, but not friendly enough to let him cash our cheques.

We moved at daylight. When we got within a mile of the shanty, one of the boys sez:

“Think he’ll expect us?”

“Not unless them two sundowners told him,” I said.

“They weren’t sundowners,” said the cook. “They was commercial travellers in beer.”

We saw Jimmy out in the road. He’d got his good coat on and his hair greased, and Rosie had tied a bit of blue ribbon round the neck of a cracked water-bottle. There was fresh chalk on the blackboard, too:

**WELCOME, DROVERS.**

Jimmy waved.

We waved back.

Then we kept on.

He ran beside the lead horses for fifty yards.

“Pull up!” he called. “Breakfast ready!”

“We’ve had breakfast,” said the boss.

“Have a drink!”

“Too early.”

“It’s never too early!”

“It is for us.”

Jimmy stopped. We travelled on. After another hundred yards we heard a horse galloping behind, and Jimmy came up on a grey mare with one stirrup shorter than the other and no hat.

“Here!” he shouted. “What’s this game?”

“What game?” said the boss.

“My sovereign!”

“What sovereign?”

“The sovereign I lent your men!”

“What men?”

“The two men you sent ahead.”

“We sent no men ahead.”

Jimmy’s face went quiet, which looked worse than when it was angry.

“One tall, thin blanky in a blue shirt,” he said, “and another crimson liar with a red scarf.”

“That sounds like the two that brought us your beer,” said the cook.

“My beer?”

“Very good beer,” I said. “Considering.”

Jimmy got off his mare.

“Who’s payin’ for it?”

“You said it was compliments of the house.”

“I never said— They was your men!”

“They never said they was,” said the boss.

“They said they’d been with you!”

“They might have meant spiritually,” said the cook.

Jimmy’s sharp eye jumped from one face to another, while the stony eye kept a cold watch on the cattle.

“They had three drinks each,” he said, “and feeds, and a sovereign, and a gallon of beer!”

“You shouldn’t trust strangers,” said the boss.

That made Jimmy dangerous. He caught the boss’s horse by the bridle and demanded a sovereign, the price of the beer, six drinks, two feeds, use of a can, and something extra for being made a fool of.

“We’ll pay for the beer,” said the boss, “seeing we had it.”

“You’ll pay the lot!”

“We’ll pay for what we had.”

“I’ll take it out of your hide!”

The boss was a quiet man, and quiet men should be left alone. He got down, handed his reins to me, and said:

“Don’t damage him. He may want to serve travellers later.”

Jimmy swung first. His fist went past the boss and struck our cook, who wasn’t in the dispute but had always believed in settling things thoroughly. The cook hit Jimmy under the beard. Then three dogs joined in, the grey mare backed over a water-bag, and somebody’s horse started for Mulgatown with a frying-pan clattering under its belly.

It was hard to tell where the fight was for a minute. Jimmy’s cold eye misled us. You’d think he was looking at the cook when his good eye had picked out somebody else entirely. He planted me in the ribs without once appearing to notice me, and then he rushed the boss and they rolled into a patch of burr.

At last we got him on his feet. His coat was split, his beard was full of grass-seed, and his nose pointed a shade farther west.

The boss gave him the price of the gallon.

“That’s for the beer,” he said.

Jimmy threw the money in the dust.

“I want justice!”

“You can pick it up when you find some,” said the cook.

We moved on.

Jimmy went back to the shanty, and Rosie told us afterwards that he began drinking his own whisky and explaining the robbery. Each time he explained it, the sovereign grew larger. By dinner-time it was five pounds; by three o’clock Dave and Jim had held him at revolver-point and stolen the day’s takings; and by sundown they’d tried to burn the shanty with Jimmy and Rosie inside.

Then a carrier came through and told him he’d seen two men answering the description camped beyond the railway dam. Jimmy took a tomahawk, got on the grey mare, and rode into Mulgatown yelling that he was after two bushrangers.

He found a mounted constable instead.

The constable asked why he had a tomahawk. Jimmy said it was evidence. The constable asked why he was drunk. Jimmy said that was grief. Then Jimmy called the constable a Government loafer and tried to ride through the lock-up gate.

They fined him ten bob.

# The Cartographer of Lost Roads

On the morning the road vanished, Mara Venn was halfway across it.

One moment, her boots struck the familiar white stones of the King’s Way. The next, she stood ankle-deep in wet grass, with a basket of eggs balanced on one hip and no sign of the road before or behind her.

Mara did not move.

Mist hung over the valley, thinning in the early light. To the east lay the village of Bellwether: slate roofs, crooked chimneys, the square tower of Saint Orra’s. To the west, beyond a line of black pines, stood the market town where Mara had been headed.

Between the two places, there should have been a road.

There had always been a road.

She crouched and touched the ground. The grass was old and thick, beaded with dew. No wheel ruts. No buried stone. No ditch at either side. Even the hawthorn hedges that had bordered the King’s Way were gone, replaced by open meadow.

One of the eggs cracked against another.

“Perfect,” Mara whispered.

She returned to Bellwether by following the church tower. At the edge of the village, she met Old Harl driving his sheep in circles.

“Morning,” he said. “Road’s gone.”

“I noticed.”

“Thought you might. Being a cartographer.”

“I copy tax maps, Harl.”

“Still maps.”

Behind them, the sheep moved uneasily through the grass where the road should have entered the village. They seemed offended by its absence.

By breakfast, everyone in Bellwether had gathered in the square. The baker claimed the road had been stolen by foreign agents. The schoolmaster argued that roads could not be stolen because they were not objects. The baker replied that taxes were not objects either, yet the king stole those every year.

While the debate grew louder, Mara went to the council house and unrolled the district map across the long oak table.

The map was older than she was, drawn on six sheets of calfskin stitched together with red thread. Bellwether sat near the center, represented by a cluster of tiny brown roofs. Rivers curled in blue ink. Hills rose in shaded humps. The King’s Way crossed the valley in a confident gray line.

Or it had.

Now the line ended at Bellwether’s eastern boundary and resumed three miles west of the village.

Mara leaned closer. No scraping marked the parchment. No stain or tear. The road simply stopped, as though the map had never known it.

She fetched every other chart from the cabinet. The shepherds’ map, the military survey, the old pilgrimage guide nailed to the wall—all showed the same impossible gap.

A silence spread through the council house.

Mayor Foss, who had followed her inside, removed his hat.

“Can you put it back?” he asked.

“On the map?”

“Outside.”

Mara looked at him.

He cleared his throat. “You are the village cartographer.”

“I’m the village clerk. My father was the cartographer.”

“And he trained you.”

“He trained me to sharpen quills and calculate field boundaries.”

“Well,” said the mayor, “perhaps roads are mostly field boundaries laid flat.”

By noon, Bellwether had become an island.

The northern footpath to Saint Orra’s Well disappeared next. A boy watched it happen. He said the stones had faded beneath his feet like breath from glass.

Then the mill track vanished. Then the narrow lane leading to the lower farms. Whenever a path disappeared from the earth, it vanished from every map as well.

By evening, there was no marked route out of Bellwether.

People tried leaving across the fields. They could walk toward the neighboring villages, but after an hour they found themselves approaching Bellwether from the opposite side, tired and bewildered. The sun remained in the proper place. The river flowed in its proper direction. Only distance had become treacherous.

“We are cursed,” announced Mother Elian, the priest, after the fourth group returned.

“By whom?” asked the mayor.

Mother Elian looked around the crowded square. “That remains unclear.”

“Can we be cursed by someone specific?” the baker asked. “It would help with morale.”

Mara slipped away before the meeting ended. Her cottage stood at the village edge, where the King’s Way had once passed her garden wall. She entered her father’s workroom and lit three lamps.

Edrin Venn had been dead for nine years, but the room still smelled of cedar shavings, lamp oil, and the sharp iron scent of ink. His instruments remained in their drawers: brass dividers, rulers of bone, a compass with a cracked glass face. Rolled maps filled pigeonholes from floor to ceiling.

Her father had believed maps were promises.

“A map says, ‘You are here,’” he had told Mara when she was seven. “And it says, ‘There is a way to somewhere else.’ Never draw one unless you mean both things.”

He had traveled for months at a time, returning muddy, sunburned, and full of stories. In his final years, however, he had stopped traveling. He spent long nights in the workroom drawing maps he refused to show anyone.

Mara began opening drawers.

Near midnight, she found a key taped beneath his desk. It unlocked a cedar chest hidden behind a row of obsolete land registers.

Inside lay a single map.

It showed Bellwether and the surrounding valley, but not as Mara knew them. Some roads crossed rivers without bridges. Others wound into hills and emerged miles away. Several villages appeared that no tax record mentioned. In the northern forest, her father had drawn a black door between two trees.

Across the bottom, in his narrow handwriting, were the words:

**ROADS DO NOT LEAD TO PLACES. THEY LEAD TO THE MEMORY OF PLACES.**

Beneath that:

**If Bellwether is ever forgotten, follow the road that was never built.**

Mara stared until the letters blurred.

The road that was never built was easy to find. Her father had drawn it in green ink, beginning behind their cottage and running north into the forest. No road had ever stood there. The ground rose too steeply, and a wall of granite split the hillside.

At dawn, Mara packed bread, cheese, a water flask, her father’s compass, and the strange map. Mayor Foss insisted on accompanying her. So did Mother Elian. Mara refused them both.

“If I don’t return by tomorrow,” she said, “try not to forget me.”

The mayor laughed, then stopped when she did not.

She stepped behind the cottage and opened the map.

The green road shimmered on the parchment.

Ahead, the hillside changed.

It happened without thunder or light. Ferns leaned aside. Stones rolled into the earth. A narrow trail appeared, carpeted with pine needles and climbing between the trees.

Mara looked back. Half the village watched from her garden gate.

“Do you see it?” she asked.

“See what?” called the mayor.

The trail waited.

Mara began walking.

Within twenty steps, Bellwether disappeared behind her. The church tower, chimneys, and anxious villagers vanished, replaced by dense forest. The air smelled cold and ancient. Pines rose like pillars into the mist.

The trail was clearly visible beneath her boots, yet when she glanced at the map, the green line shortened behind her. Not erased—consumed.

After an hour, she reached the granite wall. A black door stood in it.

The door had no handle, only a circular hollow at its center. Mara tried the compass. It fit perfectly.

When she pressed it into the hollow, the needle spun. The door opened inward.

Beyond was a road beneath a starless sky.

Mara hesitated on the threshold. Behind her, the green trail had almost vanished from the map. If she turned back now, she might return home. If she stepped through, there might be no return at all.

Then she remembered the empty meadow where the King’s Way had been. Bellwether’s children running across the square, delighted by a day without school. Old Harl’s sheep turning in circles.

She stepped through.

The door closed behind her.

The road was wide and paved with stones of different colors. Some shone with rain. Some were dusty with summer. Others held frost in their cracks. Along both sides stood milestones carved with names:

**HOME**

**THE SEA**

**THE HOUSE BEFORE THE FIRE**

**WHERE YOU WERE GOING WHEN YOU CHANGED YOUR MIND**

**A PLACE YOU HAVE NOT YET REGRETTED LEAVING**

Mara walked carefully.

Other roads joined and separated from hers. On one, an army marched silently backward, their banners mending themselves in the wind. On another, a woman in a red coat ran after a departing carriage that never grew closer. A path no wider than a ribbon carried a procession of children holding blue lanterns.

None looked at Mara.

At last, the road descended toward a building that stretched from horizon to horizon.

It resembled a tollhouse built by giants. Thousands of doors punctured its walls. Above the central entrance hung a sign:

**OFFICE OF LOST DIRECTIONS**

Inside, clerks sat at endless rows of desks. They wore gray coats and wrote in ledgers with white quills. The ceiling was so high that clouds drifted beneath it. Shelves climbed into those clouds, holding maps, signposts, milestones, keys, broken wheels, and jars of dust labeled in tiny script.

A clerk approached Mara.

He was a thin man with skin the color of old paper. His eyes were blue ink.

“Name?” he asked.

“Mara Venn.”

“Destination?”

“Bellwether.”

“You have come from Bellwether.”

“I’d like to go back.”

“That is not the same destination.”

He opened a ledger. “Purpose of journey?”

“To find out why our roads are disappearing.”

“Roads do not disappear.”

“They have.”

“Roads are reassigned, revoked, misremembered, surrendered, inherited, diverted, and occasionally eaten. They do not disappear.”

“Then ours have been one of those.”

The clerk sighed. “Village name?”

“Bellwether.”

He ran one finger down a column of writing.

“Bellwether, Bellwether… There are forty-three. Does yours have a silver mine?”

“No.”

“A drowned cathedral?”

“No.”

“A king sleeping under the public house?”

“Not that I know of.”

“Primary local industry?”

“Wool. Apples. Complaining.”

The clerk’s finger stopped.

“Bellwether of the Low Valley. Population four hundred and twelve?”

“Four hundred and nine.”

“Then three have already been lost.”

“Lost where?”

He closed the ledger.

“Your petition is denied.”

“I haven’t made one.”

“All petitions concerning Bellwether are denied.”

Mara seized the edge of the ledger before he could turn away.

“Why?”

The clerk’s ink-blue eyes narrowed.

“Interfering with an official record is punishable by permanent misdirection.”

“My father came here, didn’t he?”

At the mention of her father, the clerk became still.

“Edrin Venn,” Mara said. “Cartographer.”

The cloud ceiling rumbled softly.

The clerk pulled her into the space between two shelves.

“You should not say that name loudly.”

“Why?”

“He stole a road.”

Mara remembered the green line, the trail that no one else could see.

“That road?”

“No. A greater one.”

The clerk glanced around. “Come.”

He led her through aisles crowded with things lost on journeys: left gloves, farewell letters, rusted horseshoes, an entire bridge folded like paper. They passed beneath an arch made of crossroads and entered a circular room.

At its center stood a map the size of a lake.

It lay flat beneath glass, showing the kingdom in extraordinary detail. Tiny clouds cast moving shadows. Rivers flashed. Cities glimmered like beds of embers. Roads spread across the land in golden threads.

Near the center, Bellwether was a dark speck.

No golden threads touched it.

“Every place exists twice,” said the clerk. “Once in the world and once in the shared memory of the world. Roads bind the two. They carry people, goods, stories, names. When travelers stop coming, when maps cease to be read, when no one speaks of a place beyond its borders, the bond weakens.”

“People traveled through Bellwether every day.”

“Because your father committed a theft.”

The clerk pointed to a blazing road that ran from the capital to the northern provinces.

“This is the Imperial Way. Twenty-seven years ago, the king’s surveyors planned its route through the eastern valley, bypassing Bellwether. Your village would have withered. Young people would have left. The market would have closed. In time, Bellwether would have been forgotten.”

“So my father changed the route.”

“He stole the possibility of the eastern road and gave it to Bellwether. For years, travelers remembered your village because they passed through it. But stolen roads resist their shape. Your father spent the remainder of his life repairing the theft.”

“And when he died?”

“The road began to remember where it belonged.”

Mara looked at the dark speck under the glass.

“Put it back.”

“We cannot.”

“You keep every lost road in this place.”

“We keep records. We do not create remembrance.”

“Then I’ll take the road, as he did.”

The clerk recoiled. “Your father’s theft unbalanced half the kingdom. Bridges were built where rivers refused to flow. A town in the east has waited twenty-seven years for travelers who never came.”

“What happens to Bellwether?”

“It becomes inaccessible. Then uncertain. Then imaginary.”

Mara thought of the population in the ledger.

“Three people are already gone.”

“Not gone. Unremembered. Tell me their names.”

She opened her mouth.

No names came.

A coldness deeper than fear moved through her.

She pictured every house in Bellwether. The cooper’s, the smithy, the yellow cottage near the well. Between the school and Old Harl’s pasture stood an empty patch of weeds. Had there been a house there yesterday?

“Take me to whoever decides these things,” she said.

“That would be the Surveyor.”

“Take me.”

“No.”

Mara pulled her father’s map from her coat.

The clerk stared at it.

“You brought an unauthorized chart into the Office?”

“Yes.”

“Do you know what damage it could cause?”

“No, but I’m becoming interested.”

She unfolded it over the glass map.

Green light spilled across the room. Lines rose from the parchment like roots seeking soil. Alarms rang in the distant halls. Clerks shouted.

A door appeared in the air.

Mara snatched the map and ran through it.

She entered a quiet room with one window.

Outside the window, roads moved across a white landscape, twisting and knotting like living veins.

The Surveyor sat at a plain wooden desk. She was an old woman with silver hair cut to her jaw. A black ruler rested beneath her hands.

“You have your father’s impatience,” she said.

“You knew him.”

“I sentenced him.”

“To what?”

“To remember every traveler displaced by his stolen road. It killed him eventually.”

Mara approached the desk. “Bellwether did not steal anything.”

“Places survive on the choices of people. Your father denied thousands a choice to preserve four hundred.”

“He gave us twenty-seven years.”

“And spent them trying to solve the problem he created.”

The Surveyor opened a drawer and removed a bundle of letters tied with blue string. They were all addressed to Mara.

She took the top one. Her name was written in her father’s hand.

“Why didn’t I receive these?”

“Because he wrote them from places that never existed.”

Mara broke the seal.

My little lark,

Today I found a village where every house has a red door. They remember Bellwether, though none of them have been there. I think memory may not require travel. Perhaps it only requires a story that knows the way home.

She opened another.

Maps are not enough. A line on parchment can guide the feet, but only longing guides the heart.

The third letter contained a child’s drawing of Bellwether: houses with red doors, sheep taller than trees, Saint Orra’s tower leaning into a purple sky.

“Who drew this?”

“A boy in the village of Red Doors,” said the Surveyor.

“Which does not exist.”

“Not in your world.”

“But he knows Bellwether.”

“He knew your father’s stories.”

Mara looked through the window. Roads crossed and parted without end.

“My father thought stories could replace roads.”

“He hoped so.”

“Was he right?”

The Surveyor studied her. “A story is a dangerous road. It allows anyone to enter. It rarely leads them to the same place. And once built, it cannot be controlled.”

“That sounds like a road.”

For the first time, the old woman smiled.

Then the smile vanished.

“Your father failed,” she said. “He told his stories in lost places—to villages abandoned by history, to cities that might have been, to travelers who chose the wrong turning. They remembered Bellwether, but they could not anchor it to your world.”

“What would?”

“People in your world must remember it. Not as a dot on a map. They must imagine its streets. Desire its apples. Laugh at its foolishness. Mourn its losses.”

“How many people?”

“More than you can reach before Bellwether is gone.”

“Send me back.”

“To do what?”

“Tell the story.”

The Surveyor tapped the black ruler against the desk.

“A single story will not be enough.”

“Then it had better be a good one.”

The old woman looked past Mara, perhaps at some measurement no instrument could show.

“One road remains,” she said. “A temporary route. It can take you home, but only if you surrender something.”

“What?”

“Every map you have ever made.”

Mara thought of years spent bent over parchment: property lines, wells, fences, streams. The district map with her careful corrections. The small atlas she had drawn as a child. Her father’s hidden chart in her hands.

“If I surrender them, will I remember what was on them?”

“No.”

“Will I remember this place?”

“Only as a story.”

The floor shuddered. Somewhere far away, a bell rang three times.

Three more villagers forgotten.

Mara placed her father’s map on the desk.

“All of them,” she said.

The Surveyor touched the black ruler to the parchment.

Ink rose from the map in a dark cloud. At the same moment, lines vanished inside Mara’s mind. She forgot the shape of the northern forest. She forgot where the river bent. She forgot how many fields lay between Bellwether and the sea.

The loss struck like sudden blindness.

The Surveyor caught her before she fell.

“You must go now.”

A narrow road appeared outside the window, running downward into darkness.

Mara climbed onto the sill.

“Will it be enough?” she asked.

“Every true road begins as an act of faith,” said the Surveyor. “So does every false one.”

Mara stepped forward.

She landed in her garden at sunset.

The village gate stood open. Beyond it, Bellwether was fading.

The farthest cottages had become pale and transparent. The church tower flickered against the sky. People moved through the square like figures seen underwater.

Mayor Foss stared at Mara.

“Do I know you?”

“My name is Mara Venn.”

Recognition returned slowly.

“Mara,” he whispered.

“Gather everyone in the square.”

“Why?”

“I need to tell you a story.”

There were only three hundred and ninety-eight people left.

They sat on crates, doorsteps, and the rim of the dry fountain. Children huddled beneath blankets. The air tasted of frost though it was midsummer.

Mara stood where the roads had once met.

She began with an old cartographer who believed maps were promises.

She told them about the road he had stolen and the village he had saved. She told them about the Office of Lost Directions, the paper-skinned clerk, the lake-sized map, and the Surveyor measuring roads across a white world.

She told them about a boy in a village of red doors who drew sheep taller than trees because Edrin Venn had described Bellwether’s flocks as “large enough to frighten the moon.”

People laughed.

The sound seemed to strengthen the walls around them.

When Mara’s own memory failed, the villagers helped. Old Harl described the way sunlight touched the western pasture. The baker spoke of his oven, which smoked whenever rain approached. Mother Elian told how Saint Orra’s bell once rang by itself during a storm, though everyone knew she had pulled the rope and was too proud to admit it.

One by one, they made Bellwether into a story.

Then they wrote it down.

They used tax paper, flour sacks, prayer books, and the blank backs of old decrees. Every person made a copy. At dawn, the villagers tied the pages to birds.

Pigeons carried them east. Crows flew west. Children folded stories into paper boats and set them on the river, though no river path remained. The boats disappeared into the mist.

For seven days, Bellwether waited.

Seven more people vanished.

The village grew so faint that stars shone through the rooftops at night. Mara continued telling the story in the square, afraid that if she stopped, even for an hour, there would be no Bellwether when she woke.

On the eighth morning, a paper boat came floating back.

A message was written across its sail.

**To the people of Bellwether,**

**We found your story caught in the reeds near Ashcombe. Our grandmother says she visited your apple fair as a girl. She remembers a fiddler with green boots and a pie that tasted of cloves. Are you still there?**

Mara read the message aloud.

The church tower became solid.

By noon, a pigeon returned with a letter from the capital. By evening, three travelers arrived from the east, walking along a path that formed beneath their feet one stone at a time.

They had come to see whether the sheep were truly large enough to frighten the moon.

More visitors followed.

Some came because they had read the story. Others came because their parents remembered Bellwether. A bookseller arrived with twenty printed copies and sold them all in an hour. A painter came to capture the fading houses and complained when they grew solid before she finished.

The roads returned, but not as they had been.

The King’s Way remained in the eastern valley, where it had always belonged. Bellwether received narrower roads: a lane from Ashcombe, a pilgrim’s path from Saint Orra’s Well, a winding track through the northern forest.

They were inconvenient roads. Muddy roads. Roads with steep hills and poor signs.

But they were freely traveled.

Years later, Mara opened a small shop beside the square. The sign above the door read:

**MARA VENN  
CARTOGRAPHER OF PLACES THAT WISH TO BE FOUND**

She never recovered her old knowledge. She could not draw the valley from memory or calculate a boundary without walking it first. So she walked every road herself. She spoke to people along the way. She asked what they loved, what they feared, and what they wanted strangers to know.

On her maps, she marked more than bridges and distances.

Here the blackberries are sweetest after rain.

Here a woman named Sella will mend a stranger’s coat.

Here the road seems wrong, but continue.

Here you can see Bellwether’s tower at sunset.

Travelers complained that her charts were crowded and imprecise. They also kept them for years after their journeys ended.

When Mara was very old, a young apprentice asked why every map she made showed a green road running north from Bellwether into the forest.

“I’ve looked for it,” the apprentice said. “There’s nothing there but stone.”

Mara smiled.

She remembered a black door, though only as a story. She remembered an old woman with a ruler. She remembered her father’s promise.

“That road isn’t for leaving,” she said. “It is for finding your way back when all the others are gone.”

Outside, evening settled over Bellwether. Visitors filled the inns. Sheep wandered home through the western meadow. The church bell rang, and its sound traveled down every open road.

Far away, in villages Mara would never see, people looked up from their suppers and listened.

For a moment, they thought of a place with slate roofs, apple orchards, troublesome sheep, and a tower leaning into the sunset.

And because they thought of it, Bellwether remained.
